endorsements.title: Action Guide: Artificial Intelligence (AI)
endorsements.issuer: National Association of Community Health Centers
endorsements.quote: A randomized trial in a large U.S. health system demonstrated that proactive care management for at-risk patients identified by AI led to a 27% reduction in preventable hospital admissions.

evidence.title: An artificial intelligence-based model to reduce the no-show rate in outpatient clinics of an academic hospital
evidence.outcome: No-show rate among highest-risk patients randomized to reminder calls versus no call
evidence.effect: Intervention group had a 26.2% reduction in no-shows, equal to a 14.3% decrease in overall no-shows.
evidence.quote: This reduction translates to a 14.3% decrease in the overall number of no-shows, demonstrating the efficacy of the reminder service.

evidence.title: Testing a Program to Help Patients Prepare for Kidney Failure Treatment – The PREPARE NOW Study
evidence.outcome: Effect of risk-prediction-based care-management enrollment bundle on patient-reported, hospitalization, referral, and documentation outcomes
evidence.effect: Risk-flagged high-risk patients were screened for care management (71%). No improvement in empowerment, self-efficacy, or self-care choice; hospitalization RR 0.70 (0.51-0.96); referral OR 0.67 (0.33-1.33); preference documentation IRR 1.34 (1.06-1.69).
evidence.quote: In intervention clinics, uptake of the Patient-Centered Kidney Transitions Care intervention's education and self-management programs was low; however, the kidney transitions specialists screened most (n = 318 [71%]) of those classified as high risk and receiving care in intervention clinics for enrollment into care management.
evidence.sample_unit: patients in the Kidney Transitions Registry (EHR outcomes); 1473 surveyed, 836 chart-reviewed

evidence.title: Automated Calls Added to SMS Reminders Reduce Missed Appointments among High-Risk Patients
evidence.venue: NEJM catalyst innovations in care delivery
evidence.outcome: No-show and appointment completion rates with risk-targeted IVR outreach vs SMS alone
evidence.effect: No-show rate 1.7 points lower (9.6% vs 11.3%); completions 1.9 points higher (77.8% vs 75.9%); greatest effect in highest risk quartile; sustained over 6 months in 244,000 patients.
evidence.quote: The no-show rate was 1.7 percentage points lower (down to 9.6% from 11.3%), and the net number of appointment completions was 1.9 percentage points higher (up to 77.8% from 75.9%) in the group of patients who got an IVR call in addition to text message reminders than in the group of patients who got text message reminders alone.

evidence.title: Using a Machine-Learning Algorithm to Identify Palliative Care Needs in a Primary Care Population: A Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Time to palliative care consultation orders after risk-based identification and specialist-confirmed eligibility
evidence.effect: Time to 0.1% having consultation orders was 42.8 (34.5–54.2) days with the intervention versus 63.9 (46.8–90.1) days with control; posterior probability of shorter time, > 0.99.
evidence.quote: The median (95% credible interval) time to 0.1% of the population having the consultation ordered was 42.8 (34.5–54.2) days for the intervention arm and 63.9 (46.8–90.1) days for the control arm (posterior probability of a shorter time with the intervention, > 0.99; Fig. 3 ).

evidence.title: From prediction to practice: machine learning models and real-world interventions for magnetic resonance imaging appointment no-shows in a hospital setting
evidence.outcome: Appointment no-show rates following risk-targeted reminder calls versus no reminders
evidence.effect: No-show rates were 21.9% for 274 intervention appointments versus 22.0% for 460 controls (P = .48). Only 158 (57.7%) answered; 116 (42.3%) were not reached.
evidence.quote: Overall, the phone call trial showed no significant reduction in the no-show rate between the control (22.0%) and intervention (21.9%) groups ( P- value: .48), as shown in Table 2 .

evidence.title: A Risk-Prediction Platform for Acute Kidney Injury and 30-Day Readmission After Colorectal Surgery
evidence.outcome: Outcomes when risk predictions were paired with stratified interventions to route patient management
evidence.effect: Risk stratification paired with stratified interventions was associated with reduced AKI (11.3% to 8.8%) and readmission (12% to 8.9%) versus matched historical controls.
evidence.quote: In this study, we found significant reductions in postoperative acute kidney injury (AKI) and unplanned readmissions after the implementation of an algorithm based clinical decision support tool that risk-stratified populations and offered stratified interventions.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (479 risk-based treatment patients matched to 1437 historical controls)

evidence.title: AI-Driven Interventions for Imminent Hospital Admissions in Patients with End-Stage Kidney Disease: A Medicare and EMR-Based Analysis
evidence.outcome: Odds of all-cause hospitalization within 7 days after risk-triggered case review/intervention
evidence.effect: AI-driven intervention associated with 8% reduction in odds of 7-day hospitalization (OR=0.92; P=0.025); effective for scores 0.64-0.85, no significant effect above 0.85.
evidence.quote: AI-driven intervention was associated with an 8% reduction in the odds of hospitalization within 7 days (odds ratio=0.92; P=0.025).

evidence.title: Reducing Avoidable Emergency Visits and Hospitalizations With Patient Risk-Based Prescriptive Analytics: A Quality Improvement Project at an Oncology Care Model Practice
evidence.outcome: Change in ED visits and admissions after risk-prediction-driven nurse outreach
evidence.effect: Monthly ED visits per 100 OCM patients fell from 13.7 to 11.5 (18%); quarterly admissions fell from 19.5 to 17.1 (13%). This was a pre-post comparison with no control group.
evidence.quote: Per 100 unique OCM patients, monthly ED visits dropped from 13.7 to 11.5 (18%), a sustained month-over-month improvement.

evidence.title: Improving ART Retention Through Machine Learning–Guided Targeting of Interventions: A Monte Carlo Simulation Study in Lilongwe, Malawi
evidence.effect: Combined risk-targeted package increased high-risk retention to 64.0% (RR = 1.45; p < 0.001), +19.9 percentage points from 44.1% baseline.
evidence.quote: A combined intervention package produced substantially larger gains, increasing retention to 64.0% (RR = 1.45; p < 0.001), corresponding to an absolute improvement of 19.9 percentage points.

evidence.title: Predicting post-discharge complications in cardiothoracic surgery: A clinical decision support system to optimize remote patient monitoring resources
evidence.outcome: High-risk patients receiving remote monitoring equipment, model-based selection versus random allocation in simulated weekly distribution
evidence.effect: Model-based selection led to more high-risk patients receiving remote monitoring equipment than random allocation (no numbers given in the abstract).
evidence.quote: Compared to the random resource allocation, the selection of patients with respect to the outputs of the proposed model was proven beneficial, as it led to a higher number of high-risk patients receiving remote monitoring equipment.

commentary.bottom_line: Five randomized trials in real deployments suggest that risk-targeted outreach may reduce no-shows, hospitalizations, and time to palliative care consultation, though two of those trials found null or mixed results. Only one trial paired risk scores with an explicit eligibility check, and no trial reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations.

perspectives.view: Five randomized trials tested risk-targeted outreach in real deployments, and three supported it, including a 26.2% no-show reduction among highest-risk patients. The Swiss trial found 21.9% versus 22.0%, and the kidney trial found mixed outcomes. Outcomes differ across trials, and only one trial added specialist-confirmed eligibility, so inconsistency and indirectness lower certainty to moderate.

In a cluster trial, risk-flagged enrollment was associated with a hospitalization RR of 0.70 (0.51-0.96). A matched historical comparison reported AKI falling from 11.3% to 8.8% and readmission from 12% to 8.9%. A pre-post study reported 18% fewer monthly ED visits, but it had no control group, so secular trends may explain part of that change.

Delivery fidelity appears to limit effects. In the Swiss trial, 42.3% of targeted patients were not reached by phone, and in the kidney trial 71% of flagged patients were screened. An automated IVR trial of 59,994 patients reported a 1.7-point lower no-show rate, and the effect held over 6 months in 244,000 patients.

Only the kidney trial reported a named underserved group, rural patients. No trial reported results for Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy patients. Phone outreach reached 57.7% of targeted patients in one trial, which suggests that patients without reliable phone access may be missed when outreach is routed by risk score.

The IVR trial found its largest effect in the highest-risk quartile, which suggests that focusing contact on top-risk patients may stretch limited staff further. A simulation found that model-based selection sent remote monitoring equipment to more high-risk patients than random allocation, but it reported no numbers. No study reported cost or staffing effort.

The kidney trial found no gain in patient empowerment, self-efficacy, or self-care choice, although preference documentation rose (IRR 1.34). Palliative care consultation orders came sooner when risk-based identification was paired with specialist-confirmed eligibility, at 42.8 versus 63.9 days. These results suggest that faster routing may not change how patients experience their care.

commentary.research_gap: No trial compared routing by risk score plus eligibility criteria against eligibility criteria alone, and none reported cost, staff time, or effects in Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. The two simulation studies, including the Malawi ART retention model (epmc:PPR1271675), would need testing in real deployments before they could inform practice.
commentary.underserved_note: Only one trial reported a named underserved group (rural patients in the kidney trial), and no test reported inclusion of Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations. Health systems serving these groups cannot assume the reported reductions will carry over, especially where phone-based outreach reaches fewer patients.
